newsitem.title: USA: Gene found for endocrine tumor.
newsitem.headline: Gene found for endocrine tumor.

text.p: Scientists announced on Thursday they had discovered a gene that causes benign tumours in glands and contributes to deadly pancreatic cancer.

The gene for multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 (MEN1) causes multiple growths in the parathyroid and pituitary glands. It also causes islet cell tumours, which in turn can lead to pancreatic cancer.
The finding by scientists at the U.S. National Institutes of Health appears in the journal Science on Friday.
The MEN1 gene is a tumour suppressor but it is unlike other suppressor genes and therefore could lead scientists to new insights about the abnormal cell growth and division that creates cancer.
"It is unlike any human protein we have seen. It's a real black box," said Dr. Stephen Marx of the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases (NIDDK).
The gene is active throughout the body, not just in the endocrine system, which means that MEN1 mutations may turn out to have a role in other kinds of cancer as well.

Even the noncancerous tumours in the glands can cause disease by disrupting normal hormone production. Symptoms can include weak bones, kidney stones and certain severe stomach ulcers. The islet cell tumours can become malignant and lead to pancreatic cancer, which is deadly.
In addition to paving the way for new basic research into cancer and possible treatments for these endocrine growths, identification of the gene may lead to better screening for the genetic disorder.

Families at risk now have to have periodic blood tests, but if a gene test could pinpoint the individuals who are not at risk and those who did not inherit the gene, unnecessary monitoring could be dropped.
